sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe prior authorization and referral processes and distinguish them from one another.
- Explain the documentation, codes, and information required to support authorization and referral requests.
- Demonstrate timely submission, tracking, renewal, and follow-up practices that keep authorizations valid.
- Recognize common denial causes and apply front-end practices that prevent authorization- and referral-related denials.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by coordinating information and escalating clinical and coverage decisions to clinicians and billing staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Prior authorization is like asking your parent for permission to buy an expensive item before you buy it, so you know it will be paid for.

### Question 2

Precertification is just another word for the same 'ask the insurance company first' step, like 'pre-check' and 'pre-approval' meaning the same thing.

### Question 3

The insurance company checks first, like a teacher approving a field trip before the class goes, so nobody pays for something that was not allowed.

### Question 4

A predetermination is like asking the store to estimate your discount before you buy, so you have an idea but not a promise.

### Question 5

An approval is like a coupon that is only good for a certain number of uses and only until a certain date.

### Question 6

A formulary is like the menu of medicines the insurance company agrees to help pay for, with cheaper and pricier choices.

### Question 7

The doctor decides what care is needed, and the assistant does the paperwork, like the chef deciding the recipe while the helper gathers the ingredients.

### Question 8

Keeping notes of who you talked to and what they said is like writing down the name of the customer-service person so you can follow up later.

### Question 9

Using the online portal is like ordering with an app instead of mailing a paper form; it is faster and you can track it.

### Question 10

Starting early is like booking your trip well before vacation so nothing gets left to the last minute.

### Question 11

If a fire alarm rings, you do not wait for a normal permission slip; you use the emergency route and call for help.

### Question 12

A timely filing limit is like the last day to turn in a receipt for reimbursement; miss it and you lose the chance.

### Question 13

If your library card allows six books and you need two more, you ask the librarian for an extension, not sneak books out.

### Question 14

Checking coverage first is like confirming your ticket is valid before you get in line.

### Question 15

Missing authorization is like forgetting to get the teacher's signature; that one missing step can ruin the whole thing.

### Question 16

Do not go through the toll booth without a pass; pull over and sort it out first.

### Question 17

Documenting an appeal is like keeping your receipt and notes when you dispute a charge.

### Question 18

If someone asks a question outside your job, you say 'I will get the person who knows' instead of making up an answer.

### Question 19

If the store does not carry the item, you tell the person who ordered it so they can pick a different one.

### Question 20

Each insurance company has its own rulebook, like different classrooms having different homework rules.

### Question 21

Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage are like two schools with different permission-slip rules.

### Question 22

You can explain what 'pending' means, but you should not promise the pizza is free before the manager confirms.

### Question 23

Talking to the insurance company is like talking to a teacher: polite, clear, and you write down what happened.

### Question 24

Skipping the permission step usually means the bill gets sent back unpaid, like a field trip you did not get approved.

### Question 25

For the price, you point the customer to the cashier who can give the real total, not guess at it yourself.

### Question 26

If something looks wrong, you speak up to the person in charge instead of sending it out.

### Question 27

Recording both dates is like noting when the coupon was issued and when you plan to use it, so you know it will still work.

### Question 28

If the receipt number does not match, you compare your copy to theirs and fix the typo, not make up a new number.

### Question 29

If your form is sent back with a blank line, you fill in the blank and send it again.

### Question 30

That phone number is the help line for the permission-slip department; you call it to ask the rules.

### Question 31

The assistant can run the errands for the paperwork but cannot sign the doctor's decision.

### Question 32

It is a step-by-step recipe: get the order, check the rules, send the paperwork, then book the appointment.

### Question 33

If the app is down, you use the phone or a paper form instead of giving up.

### Question 34

Strong appeals are built on a full folder of dated receipts and notes, not a hazy memory.

### Question 35

If your permission slip says 'only with a helmet,' you wear the helmet or the deal is off.

### Question 36

If a required note is missing, you pause and go get the note instead of pretending it is there.

### Question 37

A consultation is like asking another teacher to look at your project and write back their thoughts, not handing the whole class over.

### Question 38

Keeping the 'sent successfully' page is like saving your proof of mailing.

### Question 39

The authorization number is the confirmation code that proves the service was pre-approved.

### Question 40

The assistant handles the forms and the doctor handles the medical thinking.

### Question 41

The NPI is like the doctor's employee ID number, so the insurance company knows exactly who ordered the service.

### Question 42

Getting the permission slips right up front is like building a strong foundation so the house does not crack later.

### Question 43

Different teachers grade by different rubrics, so you follow the rubric of the teacher whose class you are in.

### Question 44

Tracking where things go wrong is like checking the scoreboard and stats to find what to practice next.

### Question 45

If the order changes, you check whether you need a new permission slip, not assume the old one still works.

### Question 46

Good notes are like a shared to-do list so everyone knows what happened and nothing important is dropped.

### Question 47

If the limit is reached, the doctor explains why more is needed; you do not sneak extra servings onto someone else's plate.

### Question 48

You send only the pages the specialist needs, not the whole file cabinet.

### Question 49

A denial is like a 'not yet' that the doctor can often ask to have looked at again.

### Question 50

If the receipt says 'sneakers' but you ordered 'boots,' you fix the mix-up before you leave the store.
